analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from writing carbon pollution rules for power plants unless Congress explicitly authorizes them.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced days after President Obama directed the EPA to write carbon pollution standards for existing coal-fired power plants, would prohibit any federal agency from issuing those standards—or anything substantially similar—unless Congress passed a law explicitly authorizing them [S2] [S3]. In practice it would have blocked the EPA rules that became the Clean Power Plan, leaving power plant carbon emissions unregulated unless Congress acted [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, never received a vote, and died there at the end of the Congress [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, coal mining companies and electric utilities that burn coal would have been spared federal limits on their carbon emissions, avoiding the cost of retrofitting or retiring coal plants. Electricity consumers in coal-dependent regions might have avoided some near-term rate pressure, the bill's central argument for protecting households and small businesses.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal agency from issuing a power sector carbon pollution standard, or any substantially similar regulation, on or after June 25, 2013, unless Congress explicitly authorizes it in law [S2] [S3].

Was framed by its sponsors as protecting families, seniors on fixed incomes, and small businesses from higher electricity bills and job losses that they argued would result from a 'national energy tax' on power plants [S3].

Was introduced in direct response to President Obama's June 25, 2013 memorandum directing the EPA to write carbon standards for existing coal-fired power plants, which the bill said circumvented Congress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on the public in the form of continued uncontrolled carbon emissions from existing power plants—contributing to air pollution and climate change—and on cleaner energy producers who compete against coal that faces no carbon cost. The EPA's authority to regulate this pollution would have been suspended until Congress chose to act.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to power plant pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill's central objection—that limiting carbon emissions from coal plants could raise electricity prices in coal-dependent regions and affect jobs in the coal economy—is the strongest good-faith case for it, and it was the argument sponsors made in the bill's findings [S3].

The bill would have blocked not just the specific EPA rules but any 'substantially similar' regulation, indefinitely, unless Congress passed authorizing legislation—a standard that, given Congress had not passed climate legislation, would likely have meant no federal carbon limits at all for the power sector [S2] [S3].

By blocking regulation outright rather than proposing an alternative, it would have prolonged public exposure to power plant carbon pollution and left the cost of climate impacts with the general public rather than with polluters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real but narrow near-term benefit—shielding coal-dependent ratepayers and coal communities from the cost of emissions rules—while removing the only then-existing mechanism for limiting power plant carbon pollution, since Congress was not on a path to pass its own climate law. On balance it traded a broad, long-run public cost for a concentrated industry benefit, which is why its framing as a consumer-protection measure should be read alongside what it would have stopped.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barrasso introduced the bill on July 18, 2013, roughly three weeks after President Obama's June 25 memorandum directing the EPA to write carbon standards for existing coal-fired power plants [S3] [S5].
Seventeen other senators, all Republicans, cosponsored it [S4].

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on July 18, 2013; the action history shows no further action—no hearings, no markup, no floor vote—for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers and utilities burning coal were better off, since the EPA's power plant carbon standards moved forward and no Congress-passed prohibition blocked them. The public was also spared the bill's effect, since the EPA rules it targeted became the basis for the first federal limits on carbon from existing power plants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal producers; the public kept EPA rules

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without ever reaching the floor, so support and the blocking action both split along party lines.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: The bill was written to shield these industries from EPA carbon standards for existing power plants. It failed, so the rules it would have blocked moved forward, imposing compliance costs on coal-burning utilities and demand pressure on coal producers.

Had the bill passed, coal would have faced no carbon cost while renewables competed against it, weakening their relative position. The bill's failure preserved carbon rules that favor cleaner generation.

Utilities burning coal would have gained cost relief from the bill, while utilities already investing in cleaner generation faced an uneven playing field. Ratepayers in coal-dependent regions would have seen some near-term price protection, but at the cost of unregulated emissions.
